criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community access to potable water and sanitation services in urban Delhi, specifically within Kathputli Colony (piped connections, public standposts, borewells, water tankers, private vendors, and MCD paid community toilets).
criterion_notes.c2: Both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading are satisfied (plain=yes, narrow=yes). Under the plain reading, the study examines state governance, constitutional right-to-water norms (Article 21), and municipal politics of slum water provision. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it directly examines how tenure insecurity, legal recognition/notification status under Section 3 of the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956 (with pending relocation/in-situ redevelopment), utility refusal to extend formal connections for fear of legitimising slum occupancy, exclusion from 'regular customer' legal eligibility with the Delhi Jal Board (leaving residents dependent on discretionary/exceptional supply, MLA-arranged borewells, or discontinued tankers, while criminalising self-help main tapping), and user fees/closing hours at MCD community toilets directly govern and restrict household water and sanitation access.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary qualitative/socio-legal empirical case-study evidence from fieldwork in Kathputli Colony conducted from March to July 2010, comprising on-site interviews with slum residents and senior Delhi Jal Board officials, field observations, and a questionnaire survey (Note 2, p. 103), although exact sample sizes and survey tabulations are not reported. Per INCLUSION_EXCLUSION.md, qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are eligible for mechanism synthesis even without quantitative effect sizes.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete settlement- and household-level service access outcomes in Kathputli Colony, including absence of piped drinking water in Kathputli Basti (~2,500 households), dry public standposts and MCD pipes, limited borewell hard-water supply (3–4 hours/day for ~100 of 300 first-lane households), 2–3 hour summer queues at an external tap, water purchases from vendors at Rs. 5 per 1-litre can, termination of DJB tanker deliveries, informal household connections via punctured mains in Bihari Camp, and avoidance of paid MCD toilets in favour of open drains.
criterion_notes.c5: Identifies the population and units of analysis (households/residents and sub-camps within Kathputli Colony, Shadipur, Delhi, plus DJB utility officials), the legal/administrative exposures (tenure/relocation status, exclusion from regular DJB customer status, discretionary supply/tanker withdrawal, and MCD toilet fees/hours), the water and sanitation access outcomes, and an identifiable qualitative case-study design, though exact interview/survey respondent counts are not reported.

evidence_quotes.quote: The absence of legal recognition of these settlements and the corresponding lack of tenure rights of inhabitants can be a major hurdle in the way of securing access to an improved water supply.

National and local authorities are reluctant to extend water and sanitation services to people living in slums, claiming that connecting these communities will ‘legitimise’ their presence where they are not supposed to be.
They are provided access to water, not as a part of government policies, but on exceptional grounds, such that, they are not ‘regular customers’ having legal rights.
However, the residents of Bihari Camp remain exceptions, not being regular customers of DJB, and the access to clean water for them remains a ‘claim’ not a ‘right’
On-site interview and questionnaire survey, Kathputli Colony, March 2010–July 2010.
Kathputli Basti, which has approximately 2500 households, has no drinking water pipeline and the few public water standposts mostly remain dry due to illegal tapping, among other reasons.

raw_response.exposure: Legal and administrative barriers to formal service access in informal/notified slums: lack of tenure rights and pending relocation/redevelopment under Section 3 of the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act, 1956; municipal/utility refusal to extend formal connections so as not to legitimise occupation; exclusion from 'regular customer' legal status with the Delhi Jal Board (resulting in discretionary/exceptional supply, discontinued water tankers, and illegality of self-help main tapping); and user fees (Re. 1 for women, Rs. 2 for men) and early closing hours (7–10 pm) at the MCD community toilet complex
raw_response.outcome: Household and sub-settlement drinking water and sanitation access in Kathputli Colony: lack of drinking water pipelines, dry standposts and dry MCD connections, intermittent borewell hard water (3–4 hours/day for ~100 of 300 households in the first lane), 2–3 hour summer queueing at an outside tap, reliance on private water vendors (Rs. 5 per 1-litre can), cessation of DJB tanker deliveries, informal household connections from punctured mains in Bihari Camp, and low usage of paid MCD toilets / open defecation
raw_response.population_and_sample: Households and residents of Kathputli Colony, a legally notified slum in Shadipur, Delhi (~2,500 households in Kathputli Basti and surrounding camps such as Bihari Basti and Marathi Basti), and Delhi Jal Board (DJB) officials; exact interview and questionnaire sample size not reported
raw_response.rationale: This qualitative socio-legal case study examines drinking water and sanitation access in Kathputli Colony, Delhi, based on primary fieldwork conducted from March to July 2010 (on-site interviews with residents and DJB officials and a questionnaire survey). It satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2 because it analyses rule-type legal and administrative mechanisms governing slum service access—specifically lack of tenure rights, notification and pending relocation under the Slum Areas (Improvement and Clearance) Act 1956, denial of 'regular customer' utility eligibility by the Delhi Jal Board (confining residents to discretionary/exceptional supply and criminalising informal connections), and user fees/hours at MCD toilets—and documents resulting household/community water and sanitation access, exclusion, and coping outcomes. Confidence is medium because methodological reporting of the March–July 2010 survey and interviews is brief (no respondent count reported) and much of the discussion centres on residents' negotiation strategies alongside the formal legal/administrative barriers.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative socio-legal case study (fieldwork with on-site interviews and questionnaire survey, March–July 2010)
